pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: the paper’s detailed description of the transition from intact passivation to localized corrosion linked to film breakdown (PMC9504384::web::009, PMC9504384::web::016)
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a pre-passivation cleaning modification aimed at lowering chloride-induced weaknesses in the passivation film—a factor not explicitly isolated in the paper—to test its effect on corrosion retention across different temperature regimes.

fields.hypothesis: Residual chloride contamination in the passivation film is a critical factor that promotes localized corrosion initiation; an enhanced cleaning step before passivation that more effectively removes chloride species will improve long-term corrosion protection even during high-temperature, aggressive salt exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: Q235 steel after standard pickling and passivation treatment that may retain trace chloride compounds from salt contamination or cleaning processes.
fields.intervention: Implement an additional decontamination stage (e.g., an ultrasonic cleaning in deionized water or an acid rinse optimized for chloride removal) prior to passivation.
fields.conditions: Testing under both ambient cyclic salt spray and high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) where the aggressive salt environment could activate chloride-induced corrosion mechanisms.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduction of residual chloride ions within the passivation film, which in untreated samples serve as nucleation sites for film rupture and subsequent localized corrosion.
fields.mechanism: Chloride ions embedded in or near the passivation film compromise its integrity during thermal cycling, accelerating the degradation to a rapidly growing rust layer. By ensuring a cleaner surface before passivation, the formation of a more uniform and robust protective layer is promoted, thus delaying or mitigating the transition from passivation film to full-blown corrosion (PMC9504384::web::016).
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing the enhanced cleaning will exhibit reduced localized pitting, slower transition to the second protective layer failure, and overall lower corrosion weight loss compared to conventionally processed samples under identical salt spray tests. Predicted improvements are qualitative given uncertainties in chloride removal efficiency.
fields.baseline: Q235 steel processed by the standard industrial pickling and passivation method without the enhanced cleaning step.
fields.boundary: This approach is expected to work primarily for Q235 steel where chloride retention is a significant issue. Its efficacy may be reduced if chloride contamination originates from the test medium rather than the pre-treatment.
fields.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in corrosion resistance depends on the efficiency of chloride removal and the re-contamination potential during subsequent processing; precise quantification is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel specimens: one following the standard cleaning/passivation and the other including the enhanced decontamination step. Subject both groups to identical cyclic salt spray tests under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C). Evaluate initiation sites of pitting and overall corrosion progression using weight loss measurements and microscopic surface analysis.
measurements: Corrosion weight loss over time
Microscopic (SEM) analysis of pitting density and distribution
Surface chloride quantification (e.g., via XPS or EDS) prior to exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced cleaning group shows no statistically significant reduction in localized corrosion or weight loss compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: the mechanism observed in the paper where the quality of the passive film (defect density, semiconductor properties) plays a crucial role in corrosion resistance, combined with the established concept that cerium conversion coatings improve passivation by defect healing (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::007).
pool.what_is_new: This proposal adds a secondary layer (nanolayer cerium coating) to the naturally-formed passive film on Q235 steel to actively heal microdefects, thereby offering an extra barrier for corrosion protection—a strategy not explored in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: Application of a nanolayer cerium-based conversion coating on the pre-exposed passive film of Q235 steel will heal microdefects and enhance its resistance to degradation during subsequent salt exposure across temperature regimes.
fields.material_initial_state: Q235 steel with a naturally formed passive oxide film (predominantly iron oxides with mixed valence states) created under ambient conditions.
fields.intervention: Apply a thin cerium conversion coating via immersion in a cerium salt solution (e.g., Ce(NO3)3) under controlled conditions so that Ce ions are deposited on and interact with the existing passive film.
fields.conditions: The process should be carried out at room temperature under a controlled pH to optimize Ce deposition without altering the underlying film substantially. The treated Q235 steel is then subjected to corrosion testing under both room temperature and high-temperature salt exposure (700–900 °C) environments.
fields.structural_mediator: A dual-layer structure wherein the native iron oxide passive film is augmented by a nanolayer of cerium oxides/hydroxides that fill in microcracks and pinhole defects.
fields.mechanism: Cerium ions are known to migrate into defects and precipitate as cerium oxide species, effectively blocking diffusion pathways for aggressive ions (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::007). This defect-healing mechanism enhances the adhesion and continuity of the passive film. Consequently, the protective qualities of the oxide layer are improved, which should retard both the initiation and propagation of corrosion under the dual challenges of room and high-temperature aggressive environments.
fields.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel with the cerium conversion coating is expected to show a more stable and higher corrosion potential, an increased charge transfer resistance in EIS tests, and lower mass loss upon exposure to aggressive salt conditions at both temperature regimes relative to untreated samples.
fields.baseline: Naturally passivated Q235 steel without any cerium-based treatment.
fields.boundary: The advantage of the cerium treatment depends on the uniformity and adherence of the conversion coating. In conditions where mechanical spalling or severe thermal cycling occurs, the coating might not remain intact.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements are hard to predict without initial trials, and the effect may vary with the specifics of the cerium deposition process.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one group receives the cerium conversion coating treatment and the other remains as the natural passive film control. Expose both groups to standardized aggressive salt environments under room-temperature and high-temperature regimes (700–900 °C) and monitor the corrosion progression.
measurements: Electrochemical tests (EIS, OCP) to assess passive film performance
Mass loss measurements after exposure
Surface analysis (XPS, SEM) to verify the presence and integrity of the cerium layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with the cerium layer do not display statistically significant enhancements in corrosion resistance metrics or if the coating degrades rapidly under test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: the article’s demonstration that film-based protection—achieved through synergistic passivation and adsorption—is critical for corrosion resistance, extending this concept by applying a pre-formed, high-temperature stable barrier that integrates with the native oxide.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces the use of an ultra-thin silane-based sol-gel coating to create an integrated hybrid barrier on Q235 steel, a novel approach aimed at imparting dual protection at both room temperature and high temperature without relying solely on inhibitor adsorption dynamics.

fields.hypothesis: An ultra-thin silane-based sol-gel coating applied to Q235 steel forms a chemically bonded, integrated hybrid barrier with the native oxide, reducing chloride ingress at room temperature and transforming into a stable, refractory silica network at high temperatures to limit further oxidation.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its native, irregular oxide layer and exposed metal surface.
fields.intervention: Apply an ultra-thin sol-gel coating composed of an organofunctional alkoxysilane (e.g., 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane) onto the steel surface via dipping or spraying, followed by curing at room temperature.
fields.conditions: Coating application performed under controlled ambient conditions ensuring a uniform and thin layer; subsequent tests conducted in a room-temperature alkaline chloride environment (pH ~11.5, 0.02 M NaCl) and under high-temperature salt exposures (700–900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: A hybrid organic-inorganic barrier where the silane network chemically bonds with the native iron oxide and, upon high-temperature exposure, transforms into a continuous, glassy silica (SiO2) layer integrated with the oxide.
fields.mechanism: At room temperature, the silane sol-gel enhances the continuity and adhesion of the native oxide, reducing sites for chloride attack. At high temperatures, the organic components decompose and the residual silica fuses with the native oxide to form a stable, refractory barrier that minimizes further oxidation and pitting.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated Q235 steel, samples with the silane-based coating are expected to exhibit lower corrosion current densities at room temperature and reduced mass gain, along with more uniform oxide scale morphology after high-temperature exposure. The improvements are anticipated to be moderate, with exact quantitative gains requiring optimization of the coating parameters.
fields.baseline: Q235 steel without any additional surface coating, relying solely on its native, imperfect oxide for protection.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is contingent on achieving an ultra-thin, uniform, and well-adhered sol-gel layer; if the coating is too thick or poorly bonded, it may crack or delaminate during thermal cycling.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal composition, thickness, and curing conditions of the sol-gel coating for achieving a balance between room-temperature performance and high-temperature stability remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one group is coated with the ultra-thin silane-based sol-gel and fully cured, while the other remains uncoated. Subject both sets to room-temperature alkaline chloride corrosion tests and high-temperature salt exposure (e.g., at 750 °C).
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion measurements (EIS, polarization) at room temperature
Mass gain assessments and high-temperature oxidation studies
Surface analyses (SEM, XPS) to evaluate coating integrity and oxide scale uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sol-gel coated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in reduced corrosion rates, lower mass gain, and enhanced oxide scale continuity compared to the uncoated controls, the hypothesis will be falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: the idea that the nature of the surface film (as seen in adsorption studies in PMC8226475) influences corrosion resistance, extending it to the role of pre-exposure environmental conditions on native oxide formation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces ambient storage humidity as a parameter that controls the pre-existing native oxide film quality on Q235 steel, linking it to subsequent corrosion performance under aggressive acid exposure—a factor not previously explored in the context of Q235's corrosion behavior.

fields.hypothesis: Ambient storage humidity influences the nature of the native oxide film on Q235 steel, with high-humidity pre-exposure leading to a thicker, more hydrous (and less chemically stable) oxide that is more readily dissolved in 1 M HCl, while storage in dry conditions yields a thinner, more adherent oxide that imparts slightly better corrosion resistance under both room- and elevated-temperature regimes.
fields.material_initial_state: Q235 steel as received, where the native oxide film may vary in composition and structure depending on prior environmental exposure.
fields.intervention: Expose batches of identical Q235 steel samples to controlled storage conditions: one group in a low-humidity (dry) environment and another in a high-humidity environment for a fixed period (e.g., 1 week) prior to corrosion testing.
fields.conditions: After conditioning, subject both sets to corrosion testing in 1 M HCl at room temperature (~298 K) and moderately elevated temperature (~328 K).
fields.structural_mediator: Differences in the composition and porosity of the native oxide film – a relatively anhydrous, compact oxide from dry storage versus a hydrous, loosely adherent oxide from humid storage.
fields.mechanism: High ambient humidity promotes the formation of hydrous iron oxides that are typically more porous and less chemically stable in acidic environments, thereby allowing more aggressive ion penetration and faster dissolution. In contrast, dry storage favors formation of a thinner, less hydrous oxide that, while not ideally protective, may offer a marginally better barrier against acid attack.
fields.predicted_outcome: Steel samples pre-conditioned in high-humidity conditions are predicted to exhibit higher corrosion rates and greater mass losses compared to those stored in dry conditions, as evidenced by lower polarization resistance and increased interfacial capacitance in EIS measurements at both temperature regimes.
fields.baseline: Corrosion performance of Q235 steel stored under dry conditions prior to exposure to 1 M HCl.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant only when storage conditions sufficiently modify the native oxide film; if the duration of storage is too short or if subsequent acid exposure completely removes the native film immediately, the differences may be obscured.
fields.uncertainty: The extent to which modest changes in pre-exposure humidity alter the oxide film’s protective properties under highly aggressive conditions remains somewhat unquantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Store identical batches of Q235 steel under controlled low- and high-humidity (e.g., <20% RH vs >80% RH) conditions for one week. Then, expose both groups to 1 M HCl at 298 K and 328 K for fixed durations. Compare corrosion behavior via weight loss tests and electrochemical measurements (EIS, potentiodynamic polarization), and perform surface characterization (SEM, XPS) to examine the oxide film’s condition pre- and post-exposure.
measurements: Mass loss over time
Electrochemical impedance parameters (e.g., polarization resistance, CPE values)
Surface oxide film composition and morphology (SEM, XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no measurable differences are observed in the corrosion rate or surface film characteristics between high-humidity and low-humidity stored samples under identical acid exposure conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: the observation in PMC9076090 linking activation–passivation behavior with grain-boundary dissolution, suggesting that microstructural inhomogeneities influence passivation.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces a controlled annealing step to intentionally homogenize the microstructure as a strategy to improve corrosion protection, a variable not explored in the referenced study.

fields.hypothesis: The heterogeneity at the grain boundaries of Q235 steel governs the initiation and propagation of corrosion under both ambient and high-temperature salt exposure. Homogenizing the microstructure via controlled annealing prior to exposure enhances the uniformity and robustness of the passivation layer by reducing preferential attack sites.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a heterogeneous microstructure characterized by variable grain boundary compositions and localized inclusions.
fields.intervention: Subject one set of Q235 steel samples to a controlled annealing treatment designed to homogenize the grain size and boundary chemistry without inducing additional phase changes. Compare these annealed samples to as-received, non-annealed specimens during room-temperature and high-temperature salt exposure tests.
fields.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in ambient electrochemical cells and hot-corrosion tests in salt deposits at 700–900 °C; the hypothesis applies when grain-boundary heterogeneities are significant corrosion initiation sites.
fields.structural_mediator: A uniform microstructure with reduced heterogeneity at grain boundaries mitigates localized dissolution, leading to a more uniform and adherent passive film formation.
fields.mechanism: Heterogeneous grain boundaries serve as weak links where corrosion and pitting initiate, as seen from the correlation between passivation transitions and grain boundary dissolution in PMC9076090. Annealing reduces these microstructural disparities, resulting in a passive film that is more continuous, thus improving corrosion resistance both at room temperature and under high-temperature salt stress.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel specimens are expected to exhibit lower corrosion current densities and reduced mass change during high-temperature salt exposure compared to non-annealed specimens; microscopy should reveal fewer localized corrosion pits along grain boundaries in the annealed samples.
fields.baseline: Non-annealed, as-received Q235 steel tested under the same conditions.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is operative when grain-boundary heterogeneity is the dominant factor. If the corrosion is governed by other factors (e.g., environmental aggressiveness overcoming microstructural effects), the improvement may be minimal.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in mass loss) are not precisely predicted without further microstructural analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens (annealed and as-received) and subject them to identical electrochemical and hot-corrosion tests. Use microscopy to characterize grain boundaries and mapping of corrosion pit locations. Correlate the microstructural uniformity with corrosion metrics.
measurements: Corrosion current densities (icorr) from polarization tests
Mass loss measurements in high-temperature salt baths
Grain boundary characterization via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant improvements in corrosion resistance (electrochemical stability or mass change) or show similar grain-boundary initiated corrosion sites as the as-received samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: The concept that structure (e.g., oxide film integrity) controls corrosion performance as seen in the dense Cr-rich oxides in the Ni-Cr-Mo system (PMC9100067::web::019) inspires a microstructural approach for plain steel.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis suggests altering the substrate microstructure through controlled annealing—as opposed to compositional changes or surface depositions—to indirectly improve the quality of the oxide scale and hence the corrosion protection under hot-corrosion conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Grain Refinement/Coarsening Control via Pre-corrosion Annealing to Modify Oxide Scale Pathways.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a typical fine-grained microstructure that may have high grain boundary density facilitating corrosive species penetration.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment below the austenitization temperature to induce moderate grain coarsening in the near-surface region, thereby reducing the density of grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: The intervention is carried out before any corrosive exposure. It is expected to be effective in high-temperature salt environments (above 700 °C), where grain boundaries in the oxide scale can act as rapid diffusion paths for corrosive species. The mechanism may not significantly affect room-temperature corrosion, where grain boundary diffusion is slower.
fields.structural_mediator: A coarser near-surface microstructure in the steel substrate, which promotes the formation of an oxide scale with fewer grain boundaries and defects.
fields.mechanism: Grain boundaries often serve as fast diffusion paths for oxygen, Cl–, and other aggressive ions. By reducing the grain boundary density through controlled annealing, the resultant oxide scale formed during high-temperature corrosion is expected to be more uniform and less permeable. This barrier effect reduces corrosion rates. A similar idea of controlling microstructural features to influence oxide scale integrity is observed in studies on high-temperature oxide films (e.g., as discussed in materials teaching texts on high-temperature oxidation TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028).
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel with a coarser near-surface microstructure should exhibit a more adherent and uniform oxide film with fewer defects, resulting in lower weight loss and less pitting under high-temperature salt exposure compared to as-received, fine-grained samples.
fields.baseline: Q235 steel in the as-received, fine-grained condition with a higher density of grain boundaries and, consequently, more defect-prone oxide scales.
fields.boundary: This approach may be limited by potential negative impacts on mechanical properties if grain growth is excessive and may not influence corrosion mechanisms at room temperature where diffusion rates are lower.
fields.uncertainty: The precise extent of grain coarsening required for a measurable improvement is uncertain and would need to be optimized experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one subjected to controlled annealing designed to coarsen near-surface grains and the other kept in the as-received condition. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature salt environments (700–900 °C) and compare corrosion kinetics by measuring weight loss, oxide scale uniformity (via SEM), and grain boundary mapping (via EBSD).
measurements: Weight loss per unit area
SEM and EBSD analysis of oxide scale and substrate microstructure
Pit density assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (coarser) samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity and reduced corrosion (lower weight loss and pit density) compared to the as-received samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: the observation from the paper that dissolved phosphate ions contribute to corrosion inhibition by forming protective films (PMC7794609::web::016–017) and combines it with the self-healing strategies known from other coating systems.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes an innovative, particulate-based self-healing approach for Q235 steel, where pre-applied nano-sized phosphate particles serve as an in-situ source of corrosion inhibitors—differing from both conventional conversion coatings and purely mechanical treatments.

fields.hypothesis: A nano-dispersion of phosphate particles onto the Q235 steel surface acts as a self-healing agent that, upon exposure to chloride-containing environments, slowly dissolves to release phosphate ions that react with liberated iron to form localized, protective iron phosphate precipitates.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its thin, non-uniform native oxide film.
fields.intervention: Uniformly deposit a controlled layer of nano-sized phosphate particles (e.g., ammonium dihydrogen phosphate nanoparticles) onto the steel surface, optionally followed by a light mechanical brushing to ensure adhesion without altering the substrate microstructure.
fields.conditions: Compare treated and untreated samples under room-temperature immersion in 3.5% NaCl and under a moderate thermal cycling regime (using temperatures around 350–450 °C rather than extreme 700–900 °C) to assess the self-healing behavior during both aqueous and thermal oxidative attacks.
fields.structural_mediator: A surface with finely dispersed phosphate particles that, upon initial corrosion attack, dissolve slowly to generate a local reservoir of phosphate ions, thus promoting the formation of adherent iron phosphate precipitates that ‘heal’ microcracks and defects in the native oxide layer.
fields.mechanism: Upon exposure to a corrosive environment, the nano-phosphate particles gradually dissolve; the released phosphate ions react with Fe²⁺ ions (liberated during incipient corrosion) to precipitate iron phosphate phases. This local deposition fills defects and reinforces the passive film, reducing further corrosion attack. This self-healing mechanism is conceptually similar to the additional chemical inhibition provided by dissolved phosphate in MPC coatings (PMC7794609::web::016–017).
fields.predicted_outcome: Phosphate-particle-treated Q235 steel is expected to show lower localized corrosion (manifested as fewer and smaller pits) and overall reduced corrosion rates (lower Icorr, higher Rp) relative to untreated samples, with observable formation of iron phosphate precipitates at defect sites as confirmed by surface analysis.
fields.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with only its native oxide and no additional phosphate source.
fields.boundary: Effectiveness depends on the uniformity and appropriate loading of the nanoparticles. Under conditions where the particles either dissolve too rapidly (exhausting the supply too early) or remain inert (insufficient dissolution), the self-healing effect may not manifest.
fields.uncertainty: The kinetics of phosphate release and the durability of the subsequently formed iron phosphate precipitates under prolonged and cyclic thermal exposures require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel specimens: one with a nano-dispersion of phosphate particles and one untreated. Subject both sets to room-temperature 3.5% NaCl immersion and moderate thermal cycling tests (350–450 °C cycles). Analyze surface films over time using SEM and XRD, and perform electrochemical testing to determine corrosion rates.
measurements: Electrochemical tests (Tafel polarization, LPR)
SEM imaging to detect iron phosphate precipitates
XRD for phase identification and film continuity
Mass loss and pit density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit clear formation of localized iron phosphate precipitates, and if corrosion metrics do not significantly improve relative to untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: the concept that a uniform, adherent passivation film is crucial for corrosion protection (as demonstrated in the HEA study, PMC7287792::web::014) and background knowledge linking grain refinement to improved oxide film quality.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests whether a mechanical processing approach to refine the surface microstructure of a traditional steel can mimic the corrosion protection mechanisms achieved by alloying and passivation in HEAs.

fields.hypothesis: Mechanical surface grain refinement via processes like shot peening on Q235 steel will enhance the uniformity and adherence of its native oxide layer, thereby improving corrosion protection by reducing chloride ion penetration at both room and high temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with relatively coarse surface grains and inclusions that may act as preferential sites for pitting corrosion.
fields.intervention: Apply shot peening or equivalent surface mechanical treatment to refine the grain structure and increase the density of nucleation sites for oxide formation, without introducing significant residual damage.
fields.conditions: Experiments performed in ambient and high-temperature (700–900 °C) oxidizing environments, with subsequent immersion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution to test corrosion behavior.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined near-surface microstructure with reduced grain size that fosters a more uniform and tightly adhered native oxide film.
fields.mechanism: Grain refinement increases the density and uniformity of the passive oxide film by providing more evenly distributed nucleation sites for oxidation. This uniform film, analogous in function to the dense passivation films reported for HEAs (PMC7287792::web::014), resists localized Cl– ion adsorption and diffusion by eliminating preferential pathways at coarse grain boundaries, thereby reducing pitting and mass change under corrosive conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: Shot-peened Q235 steel will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, delayed pitting initiation, and reduced mass loss during both room-temperature and high-temperature salt exposures when compared with untreated samples. The relative improvement, while directionally consistent, remains to be quantitatively established.
fields.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel that has not been mechanically modified before exposure.
fields.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the surface treatment successfully refines the grain structure without introducing excessive residual stresses or microcracks that could become corrosion initiation sites.
fields.uncertainty: While the general benefits of grain refinement on oxide film quality are known, the quantitative correlation between grain size reduction and the increase in energy barriers for Cl– diffusion remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples, one undergoing shot peening to refine the surface grain structure and one kept as a control. Analyze the surface microstructure using SEM/EBSD, then expose both groups to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and high temperature (e.g., 750 °C) for equal durations. Compare corrosion resistance via electrochemical methods and mass loss measurements.
measurements: Grain size via EBSD mapping
Electrochemical polarization curves
Mass loss after corrosion testing
Surface oxide film uniformity via SEM/XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the shot-peened samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion metrics or if the refined surface results in more pitting or increased mass loss compared to the control, then the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: The well-established oxidation resistance mechanism of alumina in high-temperature materials (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028) and the importance of controlled surface modifications for oxide scale formation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a novel surface alloying route for Q235 steel to form an alumina protective layer in situ, diverging from bulk alloy coating approaches discussed in the paper and offering a minimalist compositional intervention with a defined mechanistic basis.

fields.hypothesis: A minor surface modification by aluminum diffusion via a surface alloying process (e.g., laser surface alloying) can promote the in-situ formation of a stable and adherent Al2O3 layer that significantly enhances corrosion protection under high-temperature, salt-rich environments.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a typical low-alloy composition and a naturally formed, non-optimized oxide layer.
fields.intervention: Apply a thin surface layer enriched in aluminum (through methods like laser surface alloying or deposition followed by a brief annealing) to enable diffusion of Al into the near-surface region prior to high-temperature exposure.
fields.conditions: The Al2O3 protective mechanism is expected to be effective in oxidizing environments encountered at high temperatures (700–900°C) during aggressive salt exposure. It may have limited impact at room temperature where corrosion mechanisms differ, and the beneficial effect should be observable only if the aluminum addition is confined to the surface region.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer on the steel surface.
fields.mechanism: Alumina scales are well known for their excellent thermal stability and low oxygen permeability (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028). By enriching the surface with aluminum, upon subsequent high-temperature exposure the surface preferentially forms an Al2O3 scale rather than more volatile iron oxides. This layer reduces oxygen and salt ion diffusion, thereby mitigating corrosion. The mechanism leverages established high-temperature oxidation principles not explored in the Stellite 6 coating work.
fields.predicted_outcome: Aluminum-modified Q235 steel is predicted to exhibit substantially improved corrosion resistance, with lower mass change and more stable oxide scale formation under high-temperature salt exposure compared to unmodified Q235 steel.
fields.baseline: Unmodified Q235 steel under identical high-temperature, saline corrosion testing conditions.
fields.boundary: If the aluminum enrichment is too deep or the processing parameters are not optimized, the beneficial formation of a thin protective Al2O3 layer may not occur, or undesirable changes in other properties may result.
fields.uncertainty: While the beneficial role of Al2O3 is well established, the optimum processing conditions (depth, concentration, and thermal profile) for Q235 steel remain undefined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 steel samples with a thin, surface-enriched aluminum layer using laser surface alloying, and a control group without modification. Subject both groups to hot-corrosion testing in a salt-laden atmosphere at 800°C. Characterize the resulting oxide layers (via XRD and SEM), measure mass change, and compare corrosion rates.
measurements: XRD for oxide phase identification (looking specifically for Al2O3)
SEM imaging of the oxide layer morphology
Mass change measurement
Electrochemical corrosion testing (if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-modified samples do not exhibit the formation of a continuous Al2O3 layer or show no significant improvement in corrosion resistance compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: the common understanding that pre-existing defects in oxide films can trigger localized corrosion, and that increased temperature can hinder re-passivation kinetics (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::028).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis isolates the role of micro-cracks in the native oxide of Q235 steel and explores how elevated temperatures exacerbate their impact by preventing re-passivation, leading to localized degradation—a mechanistic angle not previously specifically addressed.

fields.hypothesis: Pre-existing micro-cracks in the native oxide film on Q235 steel serve as focal points for accelerated localized corrosion at high temperatures due to impaired re-passivation kinetics.
fields.material_initial_state: Pre‐exposed Q235 steel exhibiting intrinsic micro-cracks in its native oxide layer, arising from manufacturing and handling processes.
fields.intervention: Introduce controlled micro-indentations (to simulate micro-cracks) on the surface of Q235 steel specimens and expose them to a 95% RH neutral atmosphere at room temperature versus at 90 °C, then assess localized corrosion behavior around the defect sites.
fields.conditions: All external environmental variables (humidity, exposure duration, ambient composition) are maintained constant except that one set is exposed at room temperature while the other is at high temperature. Use of controlled indentations ensures defect presence is consistent.
fields.structural_mediator: The localized breakdown of the oxide film at micro-crack sites and the subsequent failure of effective re-passivation under high-temperature conditions.
fields.mechanism: At room temperature, even if localized defects exist, the slower oxidation kinetics allow rapid re-passivation at micro-crack edges, maintaining a relatively uniform overall oxide barrier. In contrast, at 90 °C the rapid oxidation does not allow sufficient time for re-passivation at defect sites. The micro-cracks then act as persistent channels for the ingress of oxygen and moisture, leading to accelerated localized corrosion that undermines the overall protection.
fields.predicted_outcome: Specimens with induced micro-cracks exposed at 90 °C will display markedly deeper and more extensive localized corrosion at the defect sites (observable via high-resolution microscopy) and show higher mass loss compared to similar specimens maintained at room temperature.
fields.baseline: Specimens with controlled micro-cracks exposed at room temperature under identical high-humidity conditions.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is most applicable to Q235 steel surfaces where the native oxide inherently contains micro-defects; highly polished surfaces with near-ideal oxide films may not exhibit the same behavior.
fields.uncertainty: Since the extent of micro-cracking and its impact on localized corrosion may vary with defect size and density, precise quantification of accelerated corrosion rates is somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 steel specimens and introduce standardized micro-indentation defects to simulate micro-cracks. Expose one group at room temperature and another at 90 °C in a 95% RH environment for a fixed time. Use optical and electron microscopy to examine the extent and depth of localized corrosion at the defect sites, along with overall mass loss measurements.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (optical and SEM) around induced defect sites
Electrochemical re-passivation tests to assess defect healing kinetics
Mass loss measurements for overall corrosion rate comparison
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature exposure does not result in significantly greater localized corrosion at the micro-crack sites (in terms of defect propagation or mass loss) compared to room temperature, then the hypothesis that impaired re-passivation at defects drives accelerated corrosion is disproven.

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: the observation in PMC9076090 linking activation–passivation behavior with grain-boundary dissolution, suggesting that microstructural inhomogeneities influence passivation.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces a controlled annealing step to intentionally homogenize the microstructure as a strategy to improve corrosion protection, a variable not explored in the referenced study.

fields.hypothesis: The heterogeneity at the grain boundaries of Q235 steel governs the initiation and propagation of corrosion under both ambient and high-temperature salt exposure. Homogenizing the microstructure via controlled annealing prior to exposure enhances the uniformity and robustness of the passivation layer by reducing preferential attack sites.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a heterogeneous microstructure characterized by variable grain boundary compositions and localized inclusions.
fields.intervention: Subject one set of Q235 steel samples to a controlled annealing treatment designed to homogenize the grain size and boundary chemistry without inducing additional phase changes. Compare these annealed samples to as-received, non-annealed specimens during room-temperature and high-temperature salt exposure tests.
fields.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in ambient electrochemical cells and hot-corrosion tests in salt deposits at 700–900 °C; the hypothesis applies when grain-boundary heterogeneities are significant corrosion initiation sites.
fields.structural_mediator: A uniform microstructure with reduced heterogeneity at grain boundaries mitigates localized dissolution, leading to a more uniform and adherent passive film formation.
fields.mechanism: Heterogeneous grain boundaries serve as weak links where corrosion and pitting initiate, as seen from the correlation between passivation transitions and grain boundary dissolution in PMC9076090. Annealing reduces these microstructural disparities, resulting in a passive film that is more continuous, thus improving corrosion resistance both at room temperature and under high-temperature salt stress.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel specimens are expected to exhibit lower corrosion current densities and reduced mass change during high-temperature salt exposure compared to non-annealed specimens; microscopy should reveal fewer localized corrosion pits along grain boundaries in the annealed samples.
fields.baseline: Non-annealed, as-received Q235 steel tested under the same conditions.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is operative when grain-boundary heterogeneity is the dominant factor. If the corrosion is governed by other factors (e.g., environmental aggressiveness overcoming microstructural effects), the improvement may be minimal.
fields.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in mass loss) are not precisely predicted without further microstructural analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens (annealed and as-received) and subject them to identical electrochemical and hot-corrosion tests. Use microscopy to characterize grain boundaries and mapping of corrosion pit locations. Correlate the microstructural uniformity with corrosion metrics.
measurements: Corrosion current densities (icorr) from polarization tests
Mass loss measurements in high-temperature salt baths
Grain boundary characterization via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant improvements in corrosion resistance (electrochemical stability or mass change) or show similar grain-boundary initiated corrosion sites as the as-received samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: The concept that structure (e.g., oxide film integrity) controls corrosion performance as seen in the dense Cr-rich oxides in the Ni-Cr-Mo system (PMC9100067::web::019) inspires a microstructural approach for plain steel.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis suggests altering the substrate microstructure through controlled annealing—as opposed to compositional changes or surface depositions—to indirectly improve the quality of the oxide scale and hence the corrosion protection under hot-corrosion conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Grain Refinement/Coarsening Control via Pre-corrosion Annealing to Modify Oxide Scale Pathways.
fields.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a typical fine-grained microstructure that may have high grain boundary density facilitating corrosive species penetration.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment below the austenitization temperature to induce moderate grain coarsening in the near-surface region, thereby reducing the density of grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: The intervention is carried out before any corrosive exposure. It is expected to be effective in high-temperature salt environments (above 700 °C), where grain boundaries in the oxide scale can act as rapid diffusion paths for corrosive species. The mechanism may not significantly affect room-temperature corrosion, where grain boundary diffusion is slower.
fields.structural_mediator: A coarser near-surface microstructure in the steel substrate, which promotes the formation of an oxide scale with fewer grain boundaries and defects.
fields.mechanism: Grain boundaries often serve as fast diffusion paths for oxygen, Cl–, and other aggressive ions. By reducing the grain boundary density through controlled annealing, the resultant oxide scale formed during high-temperature corrosion is expected to be more uniform and less permeable. This barrier effect reduces corrosion rates. A similar idea of controlling microstructural features to influence oxide scale integrity is observed in studies on high-temperature oxide films (e.g., as discussed in materials teaching texts on high-temperature oxidation TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028).
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel with a coarser near-surface microstructure should exhibit a more adherent and uniform oxide film with fewer defects, resulting in lower weight loss and less pitting under high-temperature salt exposure compared to as-received, fine-grained samples.
fields.baseline: Q235 steel in the as-received, fine-grained condition with a higher density of grain boundaries and, consequently, more defect-prone oxide scales.
fields.boundary: This approach may be limited by potential negative impacts on mechanical properties if grain growth is excessive and may not influence corrosion mechanisms at room temperature where diffusion rates are lower.
fields.uncertainty: The precise extent of grain coarsening required for a measurable improvement is uncertain and would need to be optimized experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one subjected to controlled annealing designed to coarsen near-surface grains and the other kept in the as-received condition. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature salt environments (700–900 °C) and compare corrosion kinetics by measuring weight loss, oxide scale uniformity (via SEM), and grain boundary mapping (via EBSD).
measurements: Weight loss per unit area
SEM and EBSD analysis of oxide scale and substrate microstructure
Pit density assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (coarser) samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity and reduced corrosion (lower weight loss and pit density) compared to the as-received samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C1
top3.builds_on: the paper’s detailed description of the transition from intact passivation to localized corrosion linked to film breakdown (PMC9504384::web::009, PMC9504384::web::016)
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a pre-passivation cleaning modification aimed at lowering chloride-induced weaknesses in the passivation film—a factor not explicitly isolated in the paper—to test its effect on corrosion retention across different temperature regimes.

fields.hypothesis: Residual chloride contamination in the passivation film is a critical factor that promotes localized corrosion initiation; an enhanced cleaning step before passivation that more effectively removes chloride species will improve long-term corrosion protection even during high-temperature, aggressive salt exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: Q235 steel after standard pickling and passivation treatment that may retain trace chloride compounds from salt contamination or cleaning processes.
fields.intervention: Implement an additional decontamination stage (e.g., an ultrasonic cleaning in deionized water or an acid rinse optimized for chloride removal) prior to passivation.
fields.conditions: Testing under both ambient cyclic salt spray and high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) where the aggressive salt environment could activate chloride-induced corrosion mechanisms.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduction of residual chloride ions within the passivation film, which in untreated samples serve as nucleation sites for film rupture and subsequent localized corrosion.
fields.mechanism: Chloride ions embedded in or near the passivation film compromise its integrity during thermal cycling, accelerating the degradation to a rapidly growing rust layer. By ensuring a cleaner surface before passivation, the formation of a more uniform and robust protective layer is promoted, thus delaying or mitigating the transition from passivation film to full-blown corrosion (PMC9504384::web::016).
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing the enhanced cleaning will exhibit reduced localized pitting, slower transition to the second protective layer failure, and overall lower corrosion weight loss compared to conventionally processed samples under identical salt spray tests. Predicted improvements are qualitative given uncertainties in chloride removal efficiency.
fields.baseline: Q235 steel processed by the standard industrial pickling and passivation method without the enhanced cleaning step.
fields.boundary: This approach is expected to work primarily for Q235 steel where chloride retention is a significant issue. Its efficacy may be reduced if chloride contamination originates from the test medium rather than the pre-treatment.
fields.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in corrosion resistance depends on the efficiency of chloride removal and the re-contamination potential during subsequent processing; precise quantification is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel specimens: one following the standard cleaning/passivation and the other including the enhanced decontamination step. Subject both groups to identical cyclic salt spray tests under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C). Evaluate initiation sites of pitting and overall corrosion progression using weight loss measurements and microscopic surface analysis.
measurements: Corrosion weight loss over time
Microscopic (SEM) analysis of pitting density and distribution
Surface chloride quantification (e.g., via XPS or EDS) prior to exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced cleaning group shows no statistically significant reduction in localized corrosion or weight loss compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.
